title: LLM-as-judge setups
summary: An LLM judge scores outputs against a rubric. The setup, not the model alone, decides reliability: pass/fail with a critique, pairwise with order swapping, reference-guided grading, rubric prompts, or several judges. Pick by the decision you are making and the stakes.
useIf: Quality is about meaning, tone or completeness that code cannot check, and you can calibrate the judge against human labels.
avoidIf: A code check or an exact reference comparison already answers the question, or you cannot spare any human labels to validate the judge.

explain.md: Strong judges agree with humans often. In the MT-Bench study GPT-4 exceeded 80% agreement, matching human-human agreement, and reached 85% against 81% among humans in the non-tie setup [[r21]]. That is a 2023 result, so validate your own judge. The setup matters more than the headline number.

items: **Pass/fail with a written critique.** Hamel Husain's critique shadowing has one principal domain expert give pass/fail judgments with critiques, then iterates the judge prompt until it agrees. He warns against uncalibrated 1 to 5 scales [[r16]].
**Pairwise.** Ask which of two answers is better. OpenAI's guidance says pairwise or pass/fail is more reliable than fine-grained scores, and to have the judge reason before it scores [[r18]].

**Reference-guided.** Give the judge the gold answer. On math questions in MT-Bench the judge failed 14 of 20 by default, 6 of 20 with chain-of-thought and 3 of 20 with a reference-guided judge [[r21]].
**Rubric or G-Eval.** Chain-of-thought plus a form-filling prompt reached a Spearman correlation of 0.514 with humans on summarization with GPT-4, with a noted bias toward LLM-generated text [[r22]].
**Several judges.** More cost, less single-model bias. Use it when stakes are high.

explain.takeaway: Gating favours pass/fail, ranking favours pairwise, checkable tasks favour a reference. Panels earn their cost only at high stakes.

explain.title: A pass/fail judge prompt (template)

explain.md: Cost is roughly items x evaluators x trials x tokens per judge call (an estimate, not a vendor formula). Levers: batch criteria in one call (Foundry `output_quality` and `tool_use_quality`), sample, validate a cheaper judge and swap order only for pairwise. Foundry's target cost view excludes evaluator model usage, so budget the judge separately [[r39]].

use: You can label 50 to 100 cases to calibrate
Binary criteria can be written clearly
avoid: Using a judge for something a regex or end-state check can verify
Trusting a 1 to 5 mean difference without an interval
Changing the judge prompt or model without re-checking agreement
flips: Gold answers exist: add them to the judge prompt
Two candidates, one decision: switch from pointwise to pairwise
Stakes rise: add order swapping, a second judge family and human review of disagreements

pitfalls.symptom: Judge scores cluster at 4 and 5 and never separate versions
pitfalls.fix: Use binary criteria with critiques and check true positive and negative rates against expert labels

pitfalls.symptom: Scores shift after a provider update with no code change
pitfalls.cause: The judge model alias or prompt changed
pitfalls.fix: Pin the judge version, store the judge prompt in version control and re-run a calibration set after any change

pitfalls.symptom: The judge favours one candidate regardless of quality
pitfalls.fix: Swap order, use a different model family and see the bias topic

scenarios.title: Choosing between two prompt versions weekly
scenarios.situation: A team iterates on a summarisation prompt and wants to know, each week, which of two candidate prompts is better. There are no reference summaries, and 300 test documents.
unknowns: How close are the candidates usually?
How many judge calls fit the budget?
scenarios.question: Which judge setup do you use?

options.name: Pairwise comparison with both orders, counting a win only if it holds both ways
options.why: It matches a ranking decision and removes position bias, at twice the calls.
options.tradeoff: Doubled cost and ties when the swap disagrees.

options.name: Score each summary 1 to 5 and compare means
options.why: A loose scale plus no interval means small differences are noise.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a quick trend check when decisions are cheap to reverse.

options.name: A panel of three judges per item
options.tradeoff: Three times the cost for a moderate-stakes decision.

flips.if: The decision becomes a release gate for one system
flips.then: Move to pass/fail criteria with a threshold.

scenarios.takeaway: Ranking two candidates is a pairwise job.

scenarios.title: Release gate over policy answers, capped budget
scenarios.situation: An assistant answers from a policy library. A CI job gates every release on 200 items. Gold answers exist for all, and the judge budget is capped.
unknowns: Which cheaper judge has been validated?
scenarios.question: How do you set up the judge?

options.name: Reference-guided pass/fail judge with critique, calibrated on an expert-labelled sample
options.why: A gate wants a binary verdict, and gold answers cut judge errors. Calibration keeps it honest.
options.tradeoff: Needs gold answers and an initial labelling effort.

options.name: Pairwise against last release
options.why: Detects regressions relative to the baseline.
options.tradeoff: Does not give an absolute pass rate and doubles calls.

options.name: A panel of five judges on every item
options.why: Cost blows the cap for a routine gate.
options.tradeoff: Panels suit rare, contested, high-stakes decisions.

flips.then: Use pass/fail criteria derived from the policy text with critique.
Add a second judge family and sampled human review.

scenarios.takeaway: A gate wants binary verdicts and references, not a panel.

quiz.q: You must rank two prompt versions with no reference answers. Which judge setup fits best?
options: Panel of five on every item
quiz.explain: Pairwise matches a ranking decision and swapping removes position bias. A 1 to 5 mean is noisy, a panel is costly for a moderate decision, and similarity to the old output rewards sameness.

quiz.q: In the MT-Bench math grading test the default judge failed 14 of 20 problems and a reference-guided judge failed 3 of 20. By how many percentage points did the failure rate fall?
quiz.explain: 14/20 = 70% and 3/20 = 15%, a fall of 55 percentage points.

quiz.q: Which choices follow the published guidance for reliable judges? Select all that apply.
options: Prefer pass/fail or pairwise over fine-grained scores
Let the judge reason before it scores
Optimise judge cost before checking agreement with humans
quiz.explain: OpenAI advises pairwise or pass/fail, reasoning before scoring, controlling length, and validating agreement with human labels before optimising cost.

flashcards.front: Why prefer pass/fail or pairwise over a 1 to 5 score?
flashcards.back: Fine-grained scales are noisy and uncalibrated. Binary or pairwise decisions are easier to define, calibrate and gate on.
One principal domain expert gives pass/fail judgments with written critiques, and the judge prompt is iterated until it agrees with them.

flashcards.front: What does a reference-guided judge change?
flashcards.back: The judge sees the gold answer. In MT-Bench math it cut judge failures from 14 of 20 to 3 of 20.
